claims.text: The alloy is produced by selective laser melting.
The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains high residual stresses and microstructural heterogeneities typical of additive manufacturing.
A post-build thermal anneal relieves the as-built residual stress.
Annealing can alter the microstructure of this alloy through second-phase precipitation and recrystallization-related evolution.
Residual stress and associated variations in grain-boundary chemistry and free volume govern diffusion pathways for reactive elements.
High residual stresses accelerate the diffusion of Cr and Ti along grain boundaries and defects.
Stress-enhanced diffusion causes Cr and Ti to segregate at the alloy surface.
Surface segregation of Cr and Ti produces a thicker, non-uniform, mechanically fragile oxide scale prone to spallation.
Stress-relieved samples have lower Cr and Ti diffusion rates than as-built samples.
Stress-relieved samples form thinner, more coherent, and more adherent oxide scales than as-built samples.
Under oxidizing conditions, annealed samples will show slower oxide growth and lower weight change than as-built samples.
Under oxidizing conditions, annealed samples will exhibit more uniform oxide morphology than as-built samples.
Comparable stress-dependent trends in oxide-scale integrity will occur under reducing H2/N2 atmospheres.
The as-fabricated alloy has notable strength and fatigue performance.
The alloy's strength and fatigue performance are attributable to its finely tuned SLM microstructure and fcc matrix.
The proposed comparison uses approximately 900 K exposures lasting 10 to 100 hours in oxidizing and reducing gases.
Failure of annealing to reduce both Cr/Ti surface diffusion and oxide-scale thickness or incoherence would falsify the residual-stress mechanism.
